lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Types of Mixtures: Homogeneous and Heterogeneous

pages.body:
Your teacher places six materials on the bench — powder, pebbles, salt, sand, oil and water. You are asked to put any two of them together. Think about what you would get.

- What happens when you mix sand and gravel? Can you tell them apart by looking?
- What happens when you mix salt and water? Can you still see the salt?
- What do you think is the difference between these two types of mixtures?

> **DEFINITION** **Mixture:** a combination of two or more substances that are physically combined but not chemically joined, and can be separated by physical means. **Homogeneous mixture:** a mixture that is uniform throughout — every part looks and behaves the same as every other part. Also called a solution. **Heterogeneous mixture:** a mixture in which the different components can be seen or detected separately — it is not uniform throughout.

[[img:igdq7g220]]

questions.q: Which of the following is the best definition of a mixture?
o: A substance formed by a chemical reaction between two elements
A combination of two or more substances physically combined but not chemically joined
A pure substance made of only one type of atom
A liquid that cannot be separated into its components
questions.e: DEFINITION Mixture: a combination of two or more substances that are physically combined but not chemically joined, and can be separated by physical means.

questions.q: A homogeneous mixture has:
o: Visible separate parts that can be distinguished by eye
Two or more distinct phases that do not mix
A uniform appearance throughout — every part looks the same
Particles large enough to be filtered out
questions.e: Homogeneous mixture: a mixture that is uniform throughout — every part looks and behaves the same as every other part.

pages.title: Homogeneous mixtures (solutions)
pages.body:
In a homogeneous mixture, the substances are so thoroughly mixed that you cannot distinguish one component from another by looking. The mixture looks the same throughout. Salt dissolved in water is a classic example. The salt particles are too small to see and are evenly spread throughout the water. Other examples include sugar solution, fresh fruit juice, vinegar solution and air (a mixture of gases).

Homogeneous mixtures have only one phase — they appear as a single, continuous material. You cannot separate the components just by picking them apart.

pages.title: Heterogeneous mixtures
pages.body:
In a heterogeneous mixture, the different components remain visually distinct. You can see or physically detect the individual parts. Sand and gravel, sand and water (before it settles), and oil and water are all heterogeneous mixtures. If you look at a handful of sand and gravel, you can see the individual grains and pebbles clearly. If you shake oil and water together, you can see two separate layers reform when it settles.

Heterogeneous mixtures have two or more phases. The components are not evenly distributed throughout the mixture.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a heterogeneous mixture?
questions.e: Sand and gravel, sand and water (before it settles), and oil and water are all heterogeneous mixtures.

questions.q: A student pours oil into water and shakes the container. After shaking, two layers form again. This mixture is:
o: Homogeneous, because the two liquids were combined
Heterogeneous, because the components remain distinct and separate
A solution, because the oil dissolved in the water
A compound, because the two liquids reacted together
questions.e: In a heterogeneous mixture, the different components remain visually distinct.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a mixture?
questions.e: If you had salt water, how would you get pure water from it?

questions.q: Vinegar is a mixture of acetic acid and water. Which type of mixture is this?
questions.e: Homogeneous mixtures (solutions)

questions.q: A mixture has only one phase and the same composition throughout. It is best described as:
questions.e: Homogeneous mixture: a mixture that is uniform throughout — every part looks and behaves the same as every other part.

pages.title: Solutes and solvents
pages.body:
When a solid, liquid or gas dissolves in a liquid to form a solution, we use specific words for each part. The solute is the substance that dissolves. The solvent is the substance that does the dissolving. The product is the solution.

For example, when you make sugar water: sugar is the solute, water is the solvent, and sugar water is the solution. Generally, the solute is present in a smaller amount and the solvent in a larger amount. Water is the most common solvent and is often called the universal solvent because it can dissolve more substances than any other liquid.

You can compare solutes and solvents by their physical characteristics. A solute is usually a solid (though it can be a liquid or gas) and appears to disappear when mixed with the solvent. A solvent is almost always a liquid and does not disappear — it remains visible as the bulk of the solution. The solute can often be recovered by evaporation of the solvent.

> **Did you know?** Air is one of the most important homogeneous mixtures in the world. It is a mixture of nitrogen (about 78%), oxygen (about 21%) and small amounts of carbon dioxide, water vapour and other gases. Because air is homogeneous, every breath you take contains the same proportions of gases regardless of where you take the breath.

> **Lesson 1 Assessment**

questions.e: Homogeneous mixture: a mixture that is uniform throughout — every part looks and behaves the same as every other part.

questions.q: In the mixture 'sugar dissolved in water', which is the solute?
questions.e: For example, when you make sugar water: sugar is the solute, water is the solvent, and sugar water is the solution.

o: It can dissolve more substances than any other liquid
It is found everywhere in the universe
It has no colour, taste or smell
questions.e: Water is the most common solvent and is often called the universal solvent because it can dissolve more substances than any other liquid.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs correctly matches a mixture type with an example?
questions.e: For example, when you make sugar water: sugar is the solute, water is the solvent, and sugar water is the solution.

questions.q: Which of the following is a physical characteristic that distinguishes a solute from a solvent?
o: The solute is always a liquid while the solvent is always a solid
The solute dissolves and appears to disappear while the solvent remains as the bulk of the solution
The solute is always present in larger amounts than the solvent
The solvent always evaporates faster than the solute
questions.e: A solvent is almost always a liquid and does not disappear — it remains visible as the bulk of the solution.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Suspensions, Colloids and the Tyndall Effect

pages.body:
Shake a bottle of groundnut paste mixed with water. It turns cloudy and milky. Leave it on the bench for ten minutes — some of the particles sink to the bottom. Now look at a glass of fresh milk. It too is cloudy and white, but if you leave it for hours it does not separate in the same way. Shine a torch through both — in one, you can see the beam of light as a glowing path; in the other, you cannot.

- What is the difference between the groundnut paste mixture and the milk?
- Why do you think the beam of light is visible in one and not the other?

> **DEFINITION** **Suspension:** a heterogeneous mixture in which large, insoluble particles are temporarily dispersed in a liquid. The particles are large enough to settle on standing and to be filtered. **Colloid:** a mixture in which tiny particles (larger than molecules but smaller than visible particles) are evenly dispersed throughout another substance. Colloid particles do NOT settle on standing. **Tyndall effect:** the scattering of a beam of light by the particles in a colloid, making the beam visible when light passes through the mixture.

questions.q: Groundnut paste mixed with water settles after a few minutes but milk does not. This difference is because:
o: Groundnut paste contains more water than milk
The particles in groundnut paste suspension are larger and settle under gravity while milk particles are colloid-sized and remain suspended
Milk is a compound while groundnut paste is a mixture
Groundnut paste is homogeneous and milk is heterogeneous

pages.title: Suspensions
pages.body: A suspension contains particles that are large enough to be seen and large enough to be filtered. When you mix groundnut paste and water and shake it, you create a temporary suspension. The particles float around for a while, making the water cloudy. But gravity eventually pulls the larger particles downward and they settle at the bottom. If you leave the mixture long enough, the water on top becomes clearer again. The Anopheles mosquito larvae in a jar of water, muddy river water and a mixture of chalk dust and water are all suspensions. You can separate the particles from a suspension using filtration — the particles are caught on the filter paper while the liquid passes through.

questions.q: A student shakes chalk dust and water in a bottle. After ten minutes, the chalk settles to the bottom. This mixture is best described as:
questions.e: A suspension contains particles that are large enough to be seen and large enough to be filtered.

questions.q: Muddy water from a river after rain is an example of:
questions.e: A suspension contains particles that are large enough to be seen and large enough to be filtered.

pages.title: Colloids
pages.body:
A colloid contains particles that are much smaller than those in a suspension but much larger than the individual molecules in a true solution. Because the particles are so small, they do not settle under gravity — they remain permanently dispersed throughout the mixture. This is why milk (fat particles dispersed in water), blood (cells and proteins in plasma), aerosol sprays (liquid droplets in air) and smoke (solid particles in air) remain mixed indefinitely.

Common examples of colloids in Ghana include milk, palm oil in water, condensed milk, fog (water droplets in air), paint and rubber latex. Colloid particles cannot be separated by ordinary filtration because they pass through most filter papers.

questions.q: Milk is an example of which type of mixture?
questions.e: Common examples of colloids in Ghana include milk, palm oil in water, condensed milk, fog (water droplets in air), paint and rubber latex.

questions.q: Why can colloid particles NOT be separated by ordinary filtration?
o: The particles are too heavy to pass through filter paper
The particles are too small to be caught by ordinary filter paper
Colloid particles dissolve in the filter paper
Colloids contain no particles at all
questions.e: Colloid particles cannot be separated by ordinary filtration because they pass through most filter papers.

pages.title: The Tyndall Effect
pages.body: The Tyndall Effect is the most reliable way to distinguish a colloid from a true solution. When a beam of light is shone through a colloid, the tiny particles scatter the light in all directions, making the beam visible as a glowing path through the liquid. This is called the Tyndall Effect.

If you shine a torch through a true solution (such as clear salt water), the beam is invisible — the dissolved particles are too small to scatter light. But if you shine the same torch through milk or through a colloid, the beam lights up as a visible streak of light. The same principle explains why a beam of sunlight coming through a dusty or smoky room is visible — the dust or smoke particles (a colloid) scatter the light and reveal the beam.

To demonstrate the Tyndall Effect in the laboratory, prepare a solution of salt water (true solution) and a colloid (milk diluted with water or gelatin solution). Shine a torch through each. Record which shows a visible beam and which does not.

questions.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of a colloid?
o: Particles are large enough to settle on standing
Particles scatter light (Tyndall Effect) but do not settle
Particles can be separated by ordinary filtration
Particles are individual molecules or ions
questions.e: In a colloid, particles are clusters of molecules — they scatter light (Tyndall Effect) but do not settle and cannot be filtered by ordinary methods.

questions.q: The Tyndall Effect is described as:
o: The ability of a solution to conduct electricity
The settling of large particles to the bottom of a suspension
The scattering of a beam of light by colloid particles, making the beam visible
The evaporation of the solvent from a solution
questions.e: Tyndall effect: the scattering of a beam of light by the particles in a colloid, making the beam visible when light passes through the mixture.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a colloid from a suspension?
o: A colloid settles on standing while a suspension does not
A colloid shows the Tyndall Effect and does not settle; a suspension does settle
A colloid can be separated by filtration while a suspension cannot
A colloid is always a gas while a suspension is always a liquid
questions.e: In a colloid, particles are clusters of molecules — they scatter light (Tyndall Effect) but do not settle and cannot be filtered by ordinary methods.

questions.q: A torch beam is shone through two liquids. In Liquid A, the beam is invisible. In Liquid B, the beam appears as a glowing streak. Which of the following conclusions is correct?
o: Liquid A is a colloid and Liquid B is a true solution
Liquid A is a suspension and Liquid B is a solution
Liquid A is a true solution and Liquid B is a colloid
Both liquids are suspensions; the difference is due to lighting conditions
questions.e: A colloid contains particles that are much smaller than those in a suspension but much larger than the individual molecules in a true solution.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an example of a colloid?
questions.e: To demonstrate the Tyndall Effect in the laboratory, prepare a solution of salt water (true solution) and a colloid (milk diluted with water or gelatin solution).

questions.q: A beam of sunlight becomes visible when entering a dusty room. This is an example of:
o: Refraction of light by the air
Diffraction of light by the window glass
The Tyndall Effect — dust particles scatter the light beam
questions.e: The same principle explains why a beam of sunlight coming through a dusty or smoky room is visible — the dust or smoke particles (a colloid) scatter the light and reveal the beam.

pages.title: Comparing solutions, colloids and suspensions
pages.body:
These three types of mixture can be distinguished by their particle size and behaviour. In a true solution, particles are individual molecules or ions — they are invisible and too small to scatter light or to filter. In a colloid, particles are clusters of molecules — they scatter light (Tyndall Effect) but do not settle and cannot be filtered by ordinary methods. In a suspension, particles are visible or nearly visible — they scatter light heavily, settle on standing and can be separated by filtration.

> **Lesson 2 Assessment**

questions.q: Which of the following correctly ranks particle size from smallest to largest?
questions.e: A colloid contains particles that are much smaller than those in a suspension but much larger than the individual molecules in a true solution.

pages.body:
Sea water contains dissolved salt. A mining company needs to separate gold particles from gravel. A community borehole pump is bringing up slightly muddy water. In each case, someone needs to get one component of a mixture back in a pure form. How would you do it?

- If you had salt water, how would you get pure water from it?
- If you had a mixture of sand and sugar, how would you separate them?
- Have you ever seen water being purified? What methods were used?

> **DEFINITION** **Sieving:** a method of separating solid particles of different sizes by passing the mixture through a mesh. Larger particles are retained; smaller ones pass through. **Filtration:** a method of separating an insoluble solid from a liquid by passing the mixture through filter paper. The solid stays on the paper; the liquid (filtrate) passes through. **Distillation:** a method of separating a dissolved solid from its solvent, or two liquids with different boiling points, by boiling and condensing the vapour. **Evaporation:** a method of separating a dissolved solid from a solution by heating until the solvent evaporates, leaving the solid behind.

questions.q: Which separation method would you use to separate sand from a mixture of sand and gravel?
questions.e: In Ghana, sieving is used in flour milling (to remove bran from flour), in quarrying (to separate gravel by size), in rice processing and in road construction.

questions.q: A sample of muddy salt water must be purified. Which sequence of methods would produce pure water?
o: Filter to remove mud, then distil to separate water from salt
questions.e: A single mixture might require more than one step — for example, muddy salt water would need filtration first to remove the mud, then evaporation or distillation to separate the salt from the water.

pages.title: Sieving
pages.body: Sieving works by exploiting the difference in particle size between components of a solid mixture. The mixture is poured onto a sieve — a mesh of a specific hole size. Particles smaller than the holes fall through; larger particles are left behind on the sieve. In Ghana, sieving is used in flour milling (to remove bran from flour), in quarrying (to separate gravel by size), in rice processing and in road construction. The key condition for sieving to work is that the particles must be dry and solid, with a clear difference in size.

pages.title: Filtration
pages.body:
Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. The mixture is poured into a funnel lined with filter paper. The filter paper has tiny pores small enough to trap solid particles but large enough to allow liquid molecules to pass through. The solid left on the filter paper is called the residue; the liquid that passes through is called the filtrate.

Filtration is used in water treatment plants to remove particles from drinking water, in laboratories to separate precipitates, in coffee making (the ground coffee is the residue; the coffee liquid is the filtrate) and in separating mud from water. Note that filtration cannot separate dissolved substances — salt water passes through filter paper because the salt particles are dissolved and too small to be caught.

questions.q: In filtration, the liquid that passes through the filter paper is called:
questions.e: The solid left on the filter paper is called the residue; the liquid that passes through is called the filtrate.

questions.q: Why can filtration NOT separate salt from salt water?
o: Salt particles are too large to pass through filter paper
Salt particles are dissolved and too small to be caught by filter paper
Salt water is too heavy to pour through a funnel
Filter paper dissolves in salt water
questions.e: Note that filtration cannot separate dissolved substances — salt water passes through filter paper because the salt particles are dissolved and too small to be caught.

questions.q: What is the key condition that must be met for sieving to separate a solid mixture?
o: The two solids must have different colours
The particles must be dry and solid with a clear difference in size
One solid must dissolve in water
The mixture must be heated before sieving
questions.e: The key condition for sieving to work is that the particles must be dry and solid, with a clear difference in size.

questions.q: The solid material left on filter paper after filtration is called:
questions.e: The solid left on the filter paper is called the residue; the liquid that passes through is called the filtrate.

pages.title: Distillation
pages.body: Distillation uses the difference in boiling points to separate a dissolved substance from its solvent, or to separate two liquids that are miscible (mix together). The mixture is heated in a flask. The liquid with the lower boiling point turns to vapour first. The vapour travels through a condenser — a glass tube surrounded by cool water — where it cools and condenses back to a liquid, which is collected as the distillate.

Simple distillation is used to separate a dissolved solid from its solvent, for example to obtain pure water from salt water. The water boils and evaporates, travels through the condenser and is collected as pure distilled water. The salt remains in the flask. Fractional distillation (a more advanced form) separates crude oil into petrol, kerosene and diesel — this is how Ghana's Tema Oil Refinery works.

questions.q: Which method does Ghana's Tema Oil Refinery use to separate crude oil into petrol, kerosene and diesel?
questions.e: Fractional distillation (a more advanced form) separates crude oil into petrol, kerosene and diesel — this is how Ghana's Tema Oil Refinery works.

questions.q: In distillation, the vapour is cooled and turned back into a liquid in which piece of equipment?
questions.e: The vapour travels through a condenser — a glass tube surrounded by cool water — where it cools and condenses back to a liquid, which is collected as the distillate.

pages.title: Evaporation
pages.body:
Evaporation is the simplest method for recovering a dissolved solid from a solution. The solution is placed in an evaporating dish and heated (or left in the sun). The solvent evaporates as a vapour into the air; the solid is left behind. Unlike distillation, the evaporated solvent is not collected.

Salt pans along Ghana's coast use evaporation to extract sea salt — sea water fills shallow ponds and the sun evaporates the water, leaving behind the salt. Evaporation is appropriate when you want to recover the solid, not the liquid.

pages.title: Choosing the right method
pages.body: The choice of separation method depends on the type of mixture and which component you want to collect. If your mixture contains solids of different sizes, sieve it. If it contains an insoluble solid and a liquid, filter it. If it contains a dissolved solid in a liquid and you want the liquid (pure water), distil it. If it contains a dissolved solid and you want the solid, evaporate it. A single mixture might require more than one step — for example, muddy salt water would need filtration first to remove the mud, then evaporation or distillation to separate the salt from the water.

questions.q: A student wants to obtain pure water from salt water. Which method is most appropriate?
questions.e: Simple distillation is used to separate a dissolved solid from its solvent, for example to obtain pure water from salt water.

questions.q: Salt farmers along Ghana's coast leave sea water in shallow pans in the sun. Which separation process are they using?
questions.e: Salt pans along Ghana's coast use evaporation to extract sea salt — sea water fills shallow ponds and the sun evaporates the water, leaving behind the salt.

questions.q: Which of the following separation methods collects the solvent (liquid) as the useful product?
questions.e: Distillation: a method of separating a dissolved solid from its solvent, or two liquids with different boiling points, by boiling and condensing the vapour.

questions.q: Which of the following is the best reason to choose evaporation over distillation for separating salt from salt water?
o: Evaporation is faster and requires no special equipment, and you want to keep the solid salt
Evaporation collects the pure water for drinking
Evaporation can separate two liquids with different boiling points
Evaporation uses a condenser to cool the vapour

pages.title: Other methods of separating mixtures
pages.body:
| **Method** | **How it works** | **Example** |
|---|---|---|
| Decantation | A heavy insoluble solid is allowed to settle and the clear liquid is poured off gently | Pouring water off washed rice, or off sand that has settled |
| Magnetic separation | A magnet attracts the magnetic material and leaves the rest behind | Removing iron filings or nails from sand |
| Winnowing | Moving air blows away the light particles while the heavy ones fall | Separating chaff from rice, maize or beans |
| Hand picking | Large unwanted pieces that can be seen are picked out by hand | Removing stones from beans or rice |
| Separating funnel | Two liquids that do not mix form layers, and the lower layer is run off through a tap | Separating palm oil or kerosene from water |
| Crystallisation | A hot, concentrated solution is cooled slowly so that pure crystals form | Obtaining sugar crystals from a sugar solution |
| Sublimation | One solid changes directly to a vapour on heating and is collected on a cool surface | Separating iodine from sand |
| Chromatography | A solvent carries different coloured substances different distances along a strip of paper | Separating the dyes in ink |

pages.title: Worked examples of separating mixtures
pages.body:
| **Mixture** | **Steps** | **Reason the method works** |
|---|---|---|
| Sand and sugar | Add water and stir to dissolve the sugar. Filter to collect the sand as the residue. Heat the filtrate gently to evaporate the water and recover the sugar | Sugar dissolves in water but sand does not |
| Sand and salt | Add water and stir. Filter to collect the sand. Evaporate the filtrate to recover the salt | Salt dissolves in water but sand does not |
| Iron filings and sand | Pass a magnet wrapped in paper over the mixture. Lift the magnet away and remove the paper to release the filings | Iron is magnetic but sand is not |
| Oil and water | Pour the mixture into a separating funnel and let it settle. Open the tap to run off the water, then collect the oil in another container | Oil and water do not mix, and oil floats on water |
| Sugar and salt | As a teacher demonstration, stir the mixture in ethanol. The sugar slowly dissolves but the salt does not. Filter to collect the salt, then warm the filtrate in a hot water bath, away from any flame, to recover the sugar | Sugar dissolves in ethanol but salt does not. Ethanol catches fire easily, so it is never heated directly |

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Writing a report on a separation

pages.title: Writing a report on a separation
pages.body:
A good report on a separation has the following parts in this order.

- Title, which names the mixture and the method.
- Aim, which states what you set out to separate.
- Materials and apparatus, listed in full.
- Method, written as numbered steps in the order they were done.
- Observations, which record what you saw at each step.
- Conclusion, which states what was separated and why the method worked.
- Precautions, which state what you did to work safely and get a good result.

> **Lesson 3 Assessment**

| **Word** | **What it means** |
|---|---|
| Mixture | A combination of two or more substances physically combined but not chemically joined |
| Homogeneous mixture | A uniform mixture that looks the same throughout; also called a solution |
| Heterogeneous mixture | A non-uniform mixture in which the different components can be detected separately |
| Solute | The substance that dissolves in a solvent to form a solution |
| Solvent | The substance that dissolves the solute; usually a liquid |
| Solution | The product formed when a solute dissolves in a solvent |
| Suspension | A heterogeneous mixture of large insoluble particles in a liquid; particles settle on standing |
| Colloid | A mixture of tiny particles dispersed throughout another substance; particles do not settle |
| Tyndall Effect | The scattering of light by colloid particles, making a light beam visible |
| Sieving | Separation of solid particles of different sizes using a mesh |
| Filtration | Separation of an insoluble solid from a liquid using filter paper |
| Residue | The solid that remains on filter paper after filtration |
| Filtrate | The liquid that passes through filter paper during filtration |
| Distillation | Separation of a dissolved solid from its solvent by boiling and condensing the vapour |
| Evaporation | Separation of a dissolved solid from its solvent by allowing the liquid to evaporate |
| Condenser | Equipment that cools vapour back into a liquid during distillation |

Liquid A is a suspension and Liquid B is a solution
Liquid A is a true solution and Liquid B is a colloid
Both liquids are suspensions; the difference is due to lighting conditions
questions.e: A colloid contains particles that are much smaller than those in a suspension but much larger than the individual molecules in a true solution.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an example of a colloid?
questions.e: To demonstrate the Tyndall Effect in the laboratory, prepare a solution of salt water (true solution) and a colloid (milk diluted with water or gelatin solution).

questions.q: A beam of sunlight becomes visible when entering a dusty room. This is an example of:
o: Refraction of light by the air
Diffraction of light by the window glass
The Tyndall Effect — dust particles scatter the light beam
questions.e: The same principle explains why a beam of sunlight coming through a dusty or smoky room is visible — the dust or smoke particles (a colloid) scatter the light and reveal the beam.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly ranks particle size from smallest to largest?
questions.e: A colloid contains particles that are much smaller than those in a suspension but much larger than the individual molecules in a true solution.

questions.q: Which separation method would you use to separate sand from a mixture of sand and gravel?
questions.e: In Ghana, sieving is used in flour milling (to remove bran from flour), in quarrying (to separate gravel by size), in rice processing and in road construction.

questions.q: A sample of muddy salt water must be purified. Which sequence of methods would produce pure water?
o: Filter to remove mud, then distil to separate water from salt
questions.e: A single mixture might require more than one step — for example, muddy salt water would need filtration first to remove the mud, then evaporation or distillation to separate the salt from the water.

questions.q: In filtration, the liquid that passes through the filter paper is called:
questions.e: The solid left on the filter paper is called the residue; the liquid that passes through is called the filtrate.

questions.q: Why can filtration NOT separate salt from salt water?
o: Salt particles are too large to pass through filter paper
Salt particles are dissolved and too small to be caught by filter paper
Salt water is too heavy to pour through a funnel
Filter paper dissolves in salt water
questions.e: Note that filtration cannot separate dissolved substances — salt water passes through filter paper because the salt particles are dissolved and too small to be caught.

questions.q: What is the key condition that must be met for sieving to separate a solid mixture?
o: The two solids must have different colours
The particles must be dry and solid with a clear difference in size
One solid must dissolve in water
The mixture must be heated before sieving
questions.e: The key condition for sieving to work is that the particles must be dry and solid, with a clear difference in size.

questions.q: The solid material left on filter paper after filtration is called:
questions.e: The solid left on the filter paper is called the residue; the liquid that passes through is called the filtrate.

questions.q: Which method does Ghana's Tema Oil Refinery use to separate crude oil into petrol, kerosene and diesel?
questions.e: Fractional distillation (a more advanced form) separates crude oil into petrol, kerosene and diesel — this is how Ghana's Tema Oil Refinery works.

questions.q: In distillation, the vapour is cooled and turned back into a liquid in which piece of equipment?
questions.e: The vapour travels through a condenser — a glass tube surrounded by cool water — where it cools and condenses back to a liquid, which is collected as the distillate.

questions.q: A student wants to obtain pure water from salt water. Which method is most appropriate?
questions.e: Simple distillation is used to separate a dissolved solid from its solvent, for example to obtain pure water from salt water.

questions.q: Salt farmers along Ghana's coast leave sea water in shallow pans in the sun. Which separation process are they using?
questions.e: Salt pans along Ghana's coast use evaporation to extract sea salt — sea water fills shallow ponds and the sun evaporates the water, leaving behind the salt.

questions.q: Which of the following separation methods collects the solvent (liquid) as the useful product?
questions.e: Distillation: a method of separating a dissolved solid from its solvent, or two liquids with different boiling points, by boiling and condensing the vapour.

questions.q: Which of the following is the best reason to choose evaporation over distillation for separating salt from salt water?
o: Evaporation is faster and requires no special equipment, and you want to keep the solid salt
Evaporation collects the pure water for drinking
Evaporation can separate two liquids with different boiling points
Evaporation uses a condenser to cool the vapour
